name: Testosterone

lead: Testosterone is the principal male sex hormone, an androgen produced mainly in the testes. It drives male secondary sexual characteristics, bone density, red blood cell production and muscle mass.

In medicine it is prescribed to treat diagnosed hypogonadism. Healthy young men given supraphysiologic doses gain muscle in a dose-dependent way, and anabolic steroid use is a feature of physique culture. Evidence of benefit is strong where there is true deficiency; use beyond that is associated with serious documented risks.

paras: Testosterone binds the androgen receptor, increasing muscle protein synthesis, satellite cell activity and bone formation, and is partly converted to estradiol and dihydrotestosterone, which have their own effects.

It is a prescription-only, controlled substance in many countries. Documented risks include suppression of natural production and fertility, acne, polycythemia, blood pressure and lipid changes, mood effects and possible cardiovascular strain; abrupt cessation can leave a deficiency. This entry is informational and not guidance for use.

lead: Testosterone is the principal male sex hormone and an androgen, a steroid hormone made mainly by the testicles in males and in smaller amounts by the ovaries in females. It drives the development of male reproductive tissues and secondary sexual characteristics, including increases in muscle and bone mass, body hair growth, voice deepening and remodelling of the jaw, brow and facial bone contours at puberty, and it also influences mood, libido, red blood cell production and metabolism.[1][2]

As a medicine, testosterone is prescribed as replacement therapy for male hypogonadism (a diagnosed deficiency), for gender dysphoria and for some breast cancers, and it appears on the World Health Organization's list of essential medicines. It can be delivered by injection, skin gel or patch, cheek tablet, nasal gel, subdermal pellet or oral capsule.[1][3] Outside medicine, supraphysiologic doses are a staple of bodybuilding and physique culture, and testosterone is discussed on strength-training forums such as T Nation, where members talk about both prescribed replacement and wider use of anabolic compounds.[4][5]

Research supports benefit from replacement in men with true deficiency, with benefit most clearly documented for sexual function, and a large randomized trial in men with hypogonadism found no excess of major cardiovascular events over placebo.[6][7] Evidence for benefit from treating age-related decline in otherwise healthy men is less settled, and non-prescribed use at high doses is associated with documented harms including suppression of the body's own hormone production and fertility.[1][8][9]

paras: Testosterone is a steroid of the androstane class that is built in several enzymatic steps from cholesterol, acts by binding and activating the androgen receptor, and is inactivated in the liver.[1] Production is regulated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis: gonadotropin-releasing hormone prompts the pituitary to release luteinizing hormone, which stimulates testicular output, and rising testosterone feeds back to dampen the signal.[2] Levels follow a daily rhythm that peaks in the morning, and average adult male levels are several times those of adult females.[1][2]

Testosterone can act directly or after conversion by 5-alpha-reductase into dihydrotestosterone, which binds the androgen receptor more strongly, or by aromatase into estradiol. Its effects are traditionally described as anabolic (muscle mass and strength, bone density and strength, linear growth and bone maturation) and androgenic (maturation of the sex organs, voice deepening, facial and body hair), though the categories overlap considerably.[1]

Before birth, testosterone and its metabolite dihydrotestosterone contribute to the differentiation of male genitalia, and prenatal androgen exposure has been linked to sex-typed behaviour. In pubertal males, sustained rises in androgen are associated with growth of the jaw, brow, chin and nose and remodelling of facial bone contours (in conjunction with growth hormone), broadening of the shoulders, expansion of the rib cage, laryngeal growth, increased sebaceous gland activity and acne.[1] These pubertal changes are the reason testosterone is often discussed in appearance-focused communities.

In adults, testosterone supports spermatogenesis, libido, red blood cell production, muscle and bone maintenance and fat distribution, and levels drift down with age, by roughly one percent a year after about age 30 according to one summary.[1][2] Low levels in men are associated with frailty, fat accumulation, depressed mood, sexual dysfunction and bone loss, whereas excessive levels have been associated with hyperandrogenism and male-pattern hair loss.[1] Low testosterone has also been associated with higher inflammatory markers, metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular risk, and studies of cognition describe a curved relationship in which both too little and too much circulating androgen may impair spatial performance.[1]

Testosterone replacement therapy aims to restore serum levels to the normal range in men with symptomatic deficiency, targeting reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, low mood, anaemia and loss of muscle and bone mass. Narrative reviews note that therapy has been in use for about seventy years and that many formulations (buccal, nasal, subdermal, transdermal and intramuscular) have been developed to improve pharmacokinetics and adherence.[3][10] Testosterone is also used in gender-affirming hormone therapy and for delayed puberty in boys.[1]

Guidelines from the American College of Physicians (2020) support discussing treatment in men with age-related low testosterone who have sexual dysfunction, with yearly review and discontinuation if there is no improvement. Whether testosterone for low levels due to ageing alone is beneficial or harmful is described as unclear in the broader literature.[1]

Healthy young men given supraphysiologic testosterone gain muscle in a dose-dependent manner, a finding established in controlled dose-response work and the basis of anabolic steroid use in bodybuilding.[4] In the looksmaxxing and physique communities, testosterone is discussed both as medically supervised 'TRT' and as a component of non-prescribed 'cycles' for muscle, leanness and what users describe as improved drive and confidence. Medical reviews of non-prescribed anabolic steroid use report that complications vary by dose, duration and compound and that users may develop symptomatic hypogonadism afterward.[8]
A large body of human research exists for testosterone, mostly in men with hypogonadism or low testosterone. This section summarises landmark and illustrative studies.

Dose-response: In a controlled study of healthy young men given graded weekly doses, testosterone produced dose-dependent increases in fat-free mass and muscle size, with strength and power changes also related to dose, while the men's own gonadal output was suppressed.[4]

Older hypogonadal men: A 12-month randomized trial of testosterone replacement in older hypogonadal men examined changes in body composition and related measures.[11] A trial in hypogonadal men with type 2 diabetes reported improved insulin resistance, glycaemic control, visceral adiposity and cholesterol with replacement.[12] Replacement in hypogonadal men has also been associated with changes in inflammatory cytokines and lipid profiles.[13]

Sexual function and symptoms: A randomized trial in men with hypogonadism reported on sexual function and hypogonadal symptoms during testosterone therapy compared with placebo, with improvements in sexual function being the best-documented effect.[7]

Cardiovascular safety: The TRAVERSE trial, a multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled non-inferiority trial, enrolled 5,246 men aged 45 to 80 with symptoms of hypogonadism, two low testosterone readings, and either existing or high risk of cardiovascular disease. It was designed to test whether testosterone replacement caused more major adverse cardiovascular events than placebo.[6] Wikipedia notes that a randomized trial found no evidence of excess major adverse cardiac events versus placebo in men with low testosterone.[1]

Prostate safety: A randomized clinical trial published in JAMA Network Open compared testosterone with placebo for high-grade prostate cancer, any prostate cancer, acute urinary retention, invasive prostate procedures and drug treatment for urinary symptoms in men with hypogonadism.[14] A systematic review focused on men with previous or active localized prostate cancer has also examined this question.[15] Wikipedia's summary is that testosterone does not appear to increase the risk of developing prostate cancer, whereas raising testosterone above castrate levels has been shown to speed progression of existing prostate cancer in men on androgen deprivation.[1]

Fertility: A 2025 review concluded that exogenous testosterone suppresses gonadotropins and intratesticular testosterone and so impairs spermatogenesis; sperm production often resumes slowly after cessation but with highly variable timing, and exogenous testosterone is contraindicated in men trying to conceive.[9]

Registered trials: ClinicalTrials.gov lists studies of testosterone replacement in heart failure patients with exercise training, in men with dysthymia, in advanced-cancer fatigue, in low-risk hormone-refractory prostate cancer, in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis and in delayed puberty, among others.[16][17][18][19]

Common side effects of testosterone medication include acne, fluid retention and breast enlargement in males; more serious effects described include liver toxicity (mainly with oral alkylated androgens, which narrative reviews say should be avoided), cardiovascular concerns, polycythemia and behavioural changes.[1][10] Accidental exposure can virilise women and children, the drug is advised against in men with prostate cancer, and it can cause harm in pregnancy and breastfeeding.[1]

Exogenous testosterone causes reversible suppression of spermatogenesis, and clinicians who treat deficiency in men wanting future fertility describe adjuncts such as human chorionic gonadotropin, selective estrogen receptor modulators or aromatase inhibitors.[10][9] A review of anabolic steroid-induced hypogonadism reports that symptomatic hypogonadism can follow non-prescribed androgen use, depending on dose, duration and compound, and that managing it may involve carefully judged replacement therapy, hCG and SERMs.[8]

Approved preparations are delivered by injection, skin delivery, buccal or nasal routes or oral formulations, and reviews compare these options by pharmacokinetics and adverse effects, and note that all approved methods, used as recommended, can restore normal serum concentrations in most hypogonadal men.[3][10][20]

Physiologically, testosterone is made in Leydig cells under luteinizing hormone control, with cholesterol conversion to pregnenolone as the rate-limiting step, and a portion is converted peripherally to dihydrotestosterone and estradiol.[2]
Testosterone is a prescription-only drug, and a controlled substance in many jurisdictions, with generic products available for approved indications.[1]

subs.h: Use in physique and looksmaxxing communities
paras: On T Nation, testosterone is discussed in dedicated 'TRT' threads, by users who report being diagnosed hypogonadal and treated for years, and in broader 'gear' discussions of stacked steroid regimens.[5][21] Some members describe competing in a 'natural' federation that allows TRT, saying the physique they reached was attainable without supraphysiologic levels.[5][21] Others in the same community argue that testosterone mainly amplifies existing traits rather than creating them, with one commenter likening the effect to a multiplier on what is there naturally.[22]

lore.intro: On strength-training forums such as T Nation, testosterone is discussed as a medical therapy ('TRT'), as a component of non-prescribed cycles, and as a determinant of physique and appearance.[5][22]

claims.claim: TRT is a legitimate long-term treatment that restores wellbeing in men with diagnosed low testosterone
Testosterone amplifies a man's existing traits ('a multiplier') rather than creating new ones
Supraphysiologic testosterone reliably builds muscle in healthy men
TRT is compatible with 'natural' bodybuilding and attainable without drugs at supraphysiologic levels
Testosterone treatment is safe for the heart and prostate
